Sound travels from the strings through the hide soundboard to the tuning pegs, and before playing the tension is adjusted with the pegs or large nails and tuned by ear until the players agree. A beginner can start with single notes on the bass and tenor and triads on the alto and soprano, then join simple harmonic progressions with arpeggios.

Its range is wide: the low register is heavy and deep, the middle the most expressive, the top clear and moving. Because the body is compact and the resonating chamber small, the volume is more restrained than a large harp's, but it produces a warm wooden tone. Its sound lies between the brilliance of the harp and the intimacy of the lyre, with the bleakness of an old instrument and a modern fineness. Compared with the modern harp the bow harp is more archaic, and it shares with the pipa a lively plucked quality, but has a soft inclusiveness that bamboo and silk instruments lack.
The bow harp (Adungu) is a chordophone, Hornbostel-Sachs number 322.11, from the traditions of the Acholi of northern Uganda and the Alur of the north-west, built from an arched resonating body with several strings. Its form represents the long musical inheritance of the two peoples, and it is called Adungu in Teso and ennanga among the Baganda. From the 1960s, because of political turmoil and efforts at cultural preservation, the instrument entered school teaching in Uganda and gradually took on a national significance. The common modern tuning, under British influence, has moved to the European major scale, while traditional practice mostly uses the pentatonic scale.

The bow harp (Adungu) is a traditional chordophone of the Acholi of northern Uganda and the Alur of the north-west, an open bow harp, Hornbostel-Sachs number 322.11. It has a hollow wooden semicircular soundbox covered with cowhide as a soundboard, and nylon strings (traditionally gut or sinew) that pass through the board and are fixed to pegs on a curved wooden frame. The sizes run from small to large, and it can be played solo, in ensemble or to accompany singing; the small one is held against the chest and plucked with both hands, the large bass set on the ground, and the player can sit on it. It is often played in quartets or quintets, mostly using arpeggios to carry the rhythm.
